summary: Defines the Layer 3 VPN Network Model, a YANG model a network controller can use to provision L3VPN services inside a service provider network. It complements the customer-facing Layer 3 VPN Service Model and gives a network-centric view. The controller uses it to derive device configuration.

plainLanguage.summary:
The L3SM describes a Layer 3 VPN as the customer sees it, which hides everything the provider has to build. The L3NM in RFC 9182 describes the same VPN from the provider's side: which routers take part, where the customer links terminate, and which routing and security settings apply.

It is a YANG module, so a controller reads and writes it over NETCONF or RESTCONF. It sits next to the L3SM rather than replacing it, and it reuses the shared definitions of the common VPN module.

questions: what is a vpn node in l3nm
subtitle: A YANG model that gives a network controller a network-side view of a Layer 3 VPN, below the customer-facing service model.

tldr.problem: The Layer 3 VPN Service Model describes a VPN from the customer's point of view and hides the provider network, so it is too abstract for a controller that must build the service and coordinate things like route targets and route distinguishers.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 9182 defines the L3VPN Network Model (L3NM), a YANG module called ietf-l3vpn-ntw. It describes each VPN service as VPN nodes, typically one per provider edge router, with network accesses, CE-PE routing, QoS, security and multicast settings, reusing the common module from RFC 9181.
tldr.outcome: A service orchestrator can use it to ask a network controller for a VPN, and a controller can derive device configuration from it. It does not replace the L3SM, and how it maps to device configuration is left to implementations.

facts.value: static, BGP, OSPF, IS-IS, RIP, VRRP

today: RFC 9182 was published in February 2022 and is a Proposed Standard. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It complements, and does not obsolete, the L3SM in RFC 8299, and it builds on the common module in RFC 9181.

sections.title: Introduction and Scope
sections.content:
The Layer 3 VPN Service Model (L3SM) of RFC 8299 describes the service a customer asks for, in the customer's terms. That abstraction limits the L3SM to the role of a customer service model.

This document defines a different model, the Layer 3 VPN Network Model (L3NM), which gives a network-centric view of Layer 3 VPN services. It lets a service orchestrator and a network controller exchange information that only the provider knows, which supports resource management and acts as a multi-domain orchestration interface where logical resources such as Route Targets and Route Distinguishers must be coordinated.

The L3NM does not obsolete the L3SM. The two serve similar goals with different scopes and views. The L3NM was first built by starting from the L3SM and pruning and extending it, but it is not defined as an augment of the L3SM, because the structure needed for network-oriented Layer 3 work is different. Some L3SM information can be passed in the L3NM, some L3SM information can be used to fill in L3NM attributes, and some L3SM information may stay local to the orchestrator, which is responsible for correlating the customer view with the network instantiation. In the other direction, information exposed by the L3NM can feed the service layer, for example to report what the network can do.

The model covers Layer 3 VPNs based on BGP provider edges, as in RFC 4364, and Multicast VPNs. It conforms to the Network Management Datastore Architecture of RFC 8342 and uses the common VPN module from RFC 9181.
sections.plainLanguage: The L3SM answers the question "what did the customer order?". The L3NM answers "what does the provider have to build?". The two sit side by side: the orchestrator holds the customer view and asks the controller for the network view.

sections.title: The Reference Architecture
sections.content:
The reference architecture expands the orchestration box of the L3SM architecture into three components: service orchestration, network orchestration and domain orchestration. The L3SM is the interface between the customer and service orchestration. The L3NM, module l3vpn-ntw, is the interface between service orchestration and network orchestration. Below that sit domain orchestration, then a configuration manager, and then the devices.

The RFC argues for a clear separation between service orchestration and network orchestration, because it gives more flexibility and follows the L3VPN reference architecture of RFC 4176. The separation relies on a dedicated interface between the components and on YANG modules that carry network-related information, and that information is hidden from customers. The translation between the customer view and the network view is implementation specific.

The same two models appear in the ACTN framework of RFC 8453, where the Customer Network Controller talks to a Multi-Domain Service Coordinator over the L3SM and the coordinator talks to a Provisioning Network Controller over the L3NM.
sections.plainLanguage: The architecture has a clear split. Service orchestration deals with the customer and uses the L3SM. Network orchestration deals with the provider's routers and uses the L3NM. Between them, a domain layer handles each part of the provider's network, and a configuration manager turns the model into device settings.

sections.title: Relationship to Other YANG Data Models
sections.content:
The L3NM reuses the identities, types and groupings of the common VPN module from RFC 9181. Early versions of the L3NM reused data nodes from the L3SM instead, but that was abandoned because it made the L3NM look as if it depended on the L3SM, which is not the case: a provider may build Layer 3 VPN services with the L3NM without exposing the L3SM to its customers.

The L3NM is not a customer service model. The internal network view may be mapped to an external customer view through the L3SM. Some parts of the L3SM map directly to the L3NM, others are generated from the requested service and local guidelines, and others are local to the provider. The design tries to align with the L3SM where it can, so that both can be used together for automated provisioning.

The topology of the VPN can be carried by a separate network topology module, such as RFC 8345. The L3NM is not a device model: once the VPN is captured, the actual provisioning uses device modules for routing, BGP, PIM, NAT, quality of service and access control lists. How the L3NM is turned into device-specific actions is implementation specific.
sections.plainLanguage: The L3NM borrows its shared definitions from the common VPN module rather than from the L3SM, so that using the network model does not imply using the service model. The network itself is described by other modules, and the L3NM says nothing about how a router is configured.

sections.title: The Structure: Profiles, Services and Nodes
sections.content:
The module ietf-l3vpn-ntw has two top-level containers. vpn-profiles holds profiles the provider maintains that apply to one or more VPN services. vpn-services holds the VPN services managed in the provider's network, each identified by a vpn-id that is meaningful only locally.

A vpn-service carries the identifier, a name, a description and the customer name, plus a parent-service-id pointing at the order that triggered it, so that the network-side service can be correlated with the service request. It has a VPN type, usually BGP/MPLS L3VPN, a topology of hub-spoke, any-to-any or custom, and a status that holds both the administrative and the operational state with the time of the last change. It also holds the underlay transport preference, the external connectivity profile, and the list of VPN instance profiles, which are reusable parameters that can be enabled at the node level.

A vpn-node is the abstraction of the policies applied on one network node, typically a provider edge, for one VPN service. It names that node with ne-id, and can carry the local AS number and the router ID. The RFC is careful to say this is an abstraction: when the node points to a specific provider edge, the node will likely map to a VRF instance, but the model also allows pointing at an abstract node, leaving the controller to decide how to split it into VRF instances. Each VPN node holds the VPN network accesses, which are the interfaces where customer traffic arrives.
sections.plainLanguage: The model has two top-level lists: profiles the provider keeps for reuse, and the VPN services themselves. Each service lists the provider's routers that take part in it, and each of those routers lists the customer links that terminate there. The model names those routers but does not say how to configure them.

sections.title: VPN Network Accesses
sections.content:
A vpn-network-access describes where one customer link reaches the VPN. It has an identifier, the interface it is bound to, a description, a type, a status, and a pointer to an active VPN instance profile, which the access inherits, although some inherited values, such as multicast, can be overridden locally.

The type tells the controller what to build. point-to-point is a direct connection between two endpoints. multipoint is a connection between the customer site and several provider edges. irb is a connection arriving from a Layer 2 VPN service, and the identifier of that service can be given. loopback is a logical interface created on a device.

The access holds six containers. connection describes the Layer 2 side: the encapsulation to use, such as 802.1Q or QinQ, a Layer 2 tunnel service such as a pseudowire, VPLS or VXLAN, a reference to the bearer that the service orchestrator allocated, and a link aggregation group. ip-connection holds the Layer 3 information, including the IP addressing, for IPv4, IPv6 or both. routing-protocols holds the CE-PE routing. oam holds the operations and maintenance settings. security holds the encryption settings or a reference to an encryption profile. service holds service parameters such as bandwidth and quality of service.
sections.plainLanguage: A network access is one customer link terminating on the provider's network. The model records what kind of link it is, how the traffic is tagged, how it is addressed, which routing protocol runs over it, and what security and service settings apply.

sections.title: CE-PE Routing, Operations and Security Settings
sections.content:
A provider can configure one or more routing protocols between the provider edge and the customer edge on a given network access. Each instance is identified separately, so several instances of the same protocol can run on one link. The protocols are static routing, BGP, OSPF, IS-IS, RIP and VRRP, and each can refer to a routing profile that holds the provider's own settings.

The RFC is explicit that the model does not include low-level policies such as filtering; those are handled at the device configuration level. It is also explicit that configuring several instances of a protocol does not by itself mean that several processes run on the device: for several BGP peers, the implementation may run one BGP process with several neighbours, several processes with one neighbour each, or a mixture.

The operations and maintenance container supports only BFD in this version, with the session flavour, the transmission and reception intervals, the multiplier, the hold time, a reference to a BFD profile and the authentication settings.

The security container controls encryption for the access: it can say whether encryption is on and at which layer, or point to a provider profile or to a customer key chain. The service container holds the bandwidth and quality-of-service settings.
sections.plainLanguage: Over each customer link the provider can run static routes, BGP, OSPF, IS-IS, RIP or VRRP, and can keep more than one instance of the same protocol on the same link. Liveness checking is limited to BFD. The model also holds the encryption settings and the bandwidth and quality-of-service settings for the link.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The module is accessed over NETCONF or RESTCONF, whose lowest layers are SSH and TLS respectively, and the Network Configuration Access Control Model of RFC 8341 is used to restrict what each user may do.

Unlike the common module, this one has writable data, and the RFC names what is sensitive. The vpn-profiles container holds data that influences how the service is delivered, so an attacker who can write to it may manipulate routing, quality-of-service or encryption settings; those nodes carry the default-deny-write tagging. In vpn-services, an attacker could delete a running service and cut off a customer's traffic, change its attributes and break the service level agreement, or create a service or add a network access. The RFC says access control helps, and that such activity can also be detected by monitoring configuration changes.

Reading is sensitive too. customer-name and the IP connection information can be used to track a customer. The keying material can be retrieved and used to inject spoofed routing advertisements. The BGP, OSPF, IS-IS, RIP and BFD nodes rely on the key chains of RFC 8177, and the module supports MD5 for the installed BGP base, which suffers from the weaknesses described in RFC 6151. The RFC also points to RFC 8915 for securing NTP inside a VPN.
sections.plainLanguage: Unlike the shared module, this one holds settings a controller writes. Someone who can write to it could delete a customer's VPN or change its encryption, so write access has to be controlled and changes have to be watched. Reading it can also leak customer names and routing keys.
